# D-ME7B5XOAG245FN65 The site is generated by chirp from the repo's Markdown and published after releases

## Context
chirp needed a public site saying what it is and how to get it, and BR wanted the repo's way of working (dev-proc) shown too. A site written by hand would be a second copy of docs that already exist in the binary and the skill.

## Decision
The site is built by chirp itself from the repo's Markdown: README, CHANGELOG, the help topics, and SKILL.md as-is behind a short intro, plus an examples page that links to commits. It is published to GitHub Pages after each tag's release succeeds, and by manual runs between releases.

## Why
Rendering the sources that already exist means the site cannot say something the binary's own docs do not. Jekyll or Hugo would add a second toolchain to a project whose point is needing nothing but chirp; bundling md4c (D-UCQGXYU3CLHRAYIT) made that unnecessary. Commit links are immutable, so the examples age but do not drift. Publishing after a release rather than on every push keeps the site describing what users can download, and running on the release's own artifact avoids building the eight-binary matrix twice. Failing the build on an unresolved link or an unknown commit makes a broken site a red run instead of a 404 someone finds later.

## Consequences
- A doc change reaches the site at the next release, or sooner by a manual run of `pages`.
- A new source file or page is added in `site/build.janet`, not by dropping a file somewhere.
- Raw HTML in the sources is rendered; they are the repo's own files, so this is trusted input.
